Elevator Pitch: A thaumaturgical sentient life-form, living deep in syberia, their culture with strong Polish influences left by Sybiraks.

item.title: Seeking Greenlight - The "Object"
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights: Yes

Page Type: SCP Article

Page Layout: I do not have a complete page layout yet, however I would add in logs and addenda of stories and experiments involving encounters with this SCP in the main article.

Elevator Pitch: SCP-xxxx is an invisible object that cannot be detected by any kind of conventional scanning ray. Once at a location, it seeks out groups of 2+ individuals engaged in conversation. It will then proceed to take the form of whatever it is the speakers are presently discussing, including living creatures. When transformed into another object/being, the SCP will behave in a fashion consistent with the speakers' perception of the object/being. If uninterrupted by another transformation, the SCP's current transformation will last one hour before it goes back to its invisible state.

Central Narrative: SCP-xxxx was found in a hospital in 198x, following originally incredulous reports from the hospital's psychiatric ward. By the time it was captured by the SCP foundation it had indirectly caused 3 casualties and directly caused 1 casualty. Descriptions of the way the casualties came to be will be included. Witnesses at the hospital have been administered Class C amnestics.

Hook/Attention-Grabber: While there are other SCPs with the ability to transform (for example, SCP-2006), the "object" does not have a particular reason for doing so. It is "benign", because it does not seek to cause harm unless the speakers are discussing something dangerous. This way, there also is the possibility that a group of people could control it and gain great power; for example, the SCP could be helpful if it is made to transform into a tool or other instrument, but it could become scary if it is made to transform into a living murderer with a knife.

Additional Notes: I am thinking that perhaps the narrative should focus more on the breadth of incidents that can be caused by this anomaly rather than the casualties per se.

item.title: Re: Hackerman B)
item.content:encoded:
Summoned by PM. My apologies for the delay.

This feels rather generic, and it's not the strongest start when you start by saying the anomaly is pretty boring. This feels like an anomalous humanoid with no real interesting traits - why spoiling the plot of something? What purpose does that serve in terms of the story and why does it matter? It feels very arbitrary and I don't see why it's here. Similarly, why is he a proficient hacker? What story purpose does this serve? There's no clear connection between the anomaly and the story here, which is a fairly big issue in a storytelling format built around a central anomaly that serves as both premise and main character.

The narrative here isn't nearly detailed enough to give us a clear sense of the quality of this idea or of what will happen in the article. We need a clearer sense of the actual events here - what information will be told to the reader and how, and why it's important. To greenlight, reviewers need confidence in the story above anything else, and to have that we need to know what actually happens.

Finally, I'm not sure why this is a format-screw. It does seem to serve any element of the idea you've described, nor does it really fit with the idea in my opinion. If you want to tell a story in first-person, you might be better writing this as a tale, but either way I'm not sure why this is a format-screw and not just a standard article. At least in my opinion, a format screw needs to be serving the story with its own format - just doing it for the sake of it usually feels a bit hollow.

item.title: Re: [Seeking Greenlight] A sentient entity formed from a psychic virus
item.content:encoded:
Summoned by PM. My apologies for the delay.

Like cybersqyd, I like the core of this. An entity formed of collective inhabitation of human minds that asks for increasingly severe demands of the Foundation is a cool premise and one with some interesting possibilities.

My main issue is that the narrative you describe right now feels like it lacks a clear escalation towards a conclusion. You've mentioned the entity asks for increasingly extreme demands, but I don't know what they are so it's difficult to have a full handle on what the escalation would look like here. Additionally, there's no ending here really. Where does the story end and why? How does that fit with the rest of the story? I think the premise here is cool but it needs to be capped with a satisfying conclusion. What is that conclusion?

I'd also second sqyd's comments on the TV show angle - it feels like an aside that doesn't fully fit with the rest of the narrative. It's tonally too different and doesn't fit well enough with the core conflict, I think.


Forum category: Writing Help / Help: Ideas Critique
Forum thread: [Seeking Greenlight] A sentient entity formed from a psychic virus

-1

I feel like there's a good core story here and I like the physical depiction and concept, but it feels like you've made a lot of incorrect assumptions that readers will be keeping up with you, resulting in a lot of basic gaps in the telling between big, swinging story moments. Much like Croquembouche says. For example, in the logs I think I as able to piece together what was going on in terms of people's locations and actions, but you omitted a lot of basic description and included some things that just made it more confusing. Ditto the line between conceptual/noosphere and reality, I never really got what was where.

A small example of a seeming disconnect: "Subjects with knowledge of SCP-5974 who have not seen the entity…"…. isn't that us, reading this file, as well as all the people discussing it in the meetings and logs?

Another example was you describing Reynes in plain terms as real, then saying that the entity looks like Reynes, and then saying they never existed. Again, I think i see what you were going for, but that kind of retrocausal fuckery is something that you have to build up and pay off, whereas here it just feels like you're saying at least three contradictory facts in the same "voice."

There's leaving room for mystery and then there's just being vague, and this is the latter. I believe you want me to be scratching my head about the Azrael connection, but I'm scratching my head about basic story elements and concepts.

I'm only downvoting on the hopes that you'll fix it. It feels like this is something you could iron out with another pass or two through it.

item.title: Re: (Seeking Greenlight) The Ancient Gateway
item.content:encoded:
Summoned by PM. My apologies for the delay.

Every event here feels motivated not by actual events, but by the desire to create the story you are creating. By that I mean, this doesn't feel like a naturally evolving story, it feels like a manufactured one. Particularly in terms of the discovery of the anomaly and it's backstory, which feels particularly built around the constraints of the already existing story. Why the events happen is explained, but don't feel particularly natural. This is a vague critique so I won't spend much time on it, but it's the biggest overarching issue for me.

As Truc Linh mentioned, this also just isn't a particularly unique story and it doesn't stand well on its own. A demigod, conflict amongst gods, "super-gods", an alternate dimension, and a containment/discovery focused narrative is a dense combination of tropes which struggle to fit together at the best of times, and don't bring anything unique or interesting to the table on their own or together. Put simply, the site audience is unlikely to be a fan of something constructed exclusively out of elements they've already seen many times before - not just seen within the SCP format either, but within fiction at large.

Finally, I want to give a little more detail on the narrative issues. What you currently have is a containment/discovery focused narrative, with a little bit of a mystery on the side. The issue there is that containment narratives are generally overdone and generic, as well as having a generally obvious core conflict that makes the tension feel lacklustre - either the Foundation does or does not contain the anomaly, but they do 99% of the time so there's far less intrigue. If you want this narrative to work, you nee dot re-centre it on the mystery of this anomaly and it's origins much more. Explore that and the questions it may raise and you'll be able to bring out a more complex, fleshed out, and engaging core conflict that is much more interesting to read.

item.title: Re: Air Reconditioning Unit
item.content:encoded:
Hi, thank you for your critique!

+ My response.
- Close response.

I’m not sure how to answer those questions and it’s mostly because I struggle with expressing the thoughts in my head. I have the answers and they make sense to me but writing them down is hard. But I’m going to try.

The whole piece is about the realisation that there’s an SCP that’s made fixing climate change kinda moot, it’s added it’s own irreversible and irrecoverable damage to the climate and that the world is kinda fucked. That’s what I want the reader to come away with.

I don’t know how I can make a character someone can relate to in this kind of piece. I thought I had at least on some small level. This one I really don’t know how to fix.

I want this to say a lot of things, like “hi I am a new writer but I want to be a part of this amazing community” or “this is something I have put time and effort and love into.” It’s probably not the right answer to that question but it’s the answer that feels right to me. This is my first SCP, when I’m gone this will remain as my legacy. I want this to be something people can point to and say “yep, that guy did that. It’s okay I guess.” That’s what I want it to say.

But again that’s not the answer you probably want, so let me try again. I love this SCP because it has potential. I make several references to another function of the object, which is functionally identical to what is described in the article except instead of turning oxygen into helium it turns it into carbon dioxide or water vapour, with the complexity going up the higher the input number. I want it to say there’s more to this, to make people think and imagine.

I did kinda stupidly think that maybe this could’ve been something that other people could collaborate on, creating and adding things to a list of what this SCP could make. But fears of it being compared to other open collaboration SCPs killed that idea. The testing log is the remnant of that I suppose, turned into an attempt to channel a narrative that admittedly has failed. I do understand that it’s a very dry narrative, and ditching the logs has been advised before. But I honestly don’t know how else to channel and describe a narrative through this kind of fiction, I’ve never written anything like an SCP article before so it’s all foreign to me.

item.title: Adoption Poster: Scribbles!
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights: No, I already have pages up

Page Type: GoI Format

Elevator Pitch: The people who adopt Scribbles always seem to have magic-related issues. When his messages get decoded, they find out he was spying on them for an avian invasion all along.

Central Narrative: Scribbles the cedar waxwing can communicate by creating and arranging sticks on the ground into words. Nobody knows where the sticks he produces come from and he never creates sticks on camera. Because he can communicate, he chooses which people adopt him — all magic users from Three Portlands.

The first person who adopts him, Maria, observes that he keeps pecking lines into a certain stick, which he hides when he notices a human looking. When she comes home to find her magical protection system disabled with beak marks in its components, she returns him.

The second owner, Robert, notices that he's pecking dots and lines in a regular pattern, almost like words. He comes home one day to find ten waxwings attempting to peck through the door to his room full of magical books. Nine of them depart when he enters. Scribbles uses his sticks to ask to be taken back to Wilson's.

The third owner, Keith, grabs Scribbles' strangely pecked stick while Scribbles is engrossed in a magic book and sends it to his friend at Anderson Robotics who specializes in cryptography.

The decoded message shows that Scribbles has been spying on humans, planning an invasion of the city (and later humanity) with his group of waxwings. The stick records his observations and is meant to be passed onto other waxwings when the right moment arrives. He's been trying to access magical areas and study magic as a way of counteracting humans' strength and technology.

Hook/Attention-Grabber: A cedar waxwing conspiracy sending a spy into Wilson's.

Additional Notes: I'm trying to decide whether this concept or my other Wilson's concept is better.

item.title: Re: Seeking Greenlight - Man in the Mirror
item.content:encoded:
[+] Open for crit

then recounting an exact replica of the events that occurred at the PCS facility, except it's an interview recounting the exact same events occurring at a SCP facility.

For a second, I thought this was going to lead into the discovery that the two organisations are the same and that there's some kinda anomaly that means some foundation sites aren't recognised as such or w/e.

I think at the end of the day, my core issue with this as a concept can be summarised as 'so what?': the impact of discovering the PCS Foundation, and the question of whether they're actually real, feels very minimal because I'm not really sure what it changes in like, my understanding of what's going on here? Like it feels like it's meant to have a big shocking moment where we realise 'oh! second foundation!' but there's no exploration of the implications of it's existence.

I'm also not necessarily convinced by this as a SCP article: what's the like, description/conprocs about? The PCS foundation? If so, the choice to have the two identical incidents happens feels even weirder because what do they actually like, add to the narrative here beyond reiterating what we already know?

item.title: Re: Dionysus Asylum
item.content:encoded:
I'm…kinda torn on this as a whole. There's some really interesting elements, and the actual setting and concept seems pretty cool; but it feels a little like you don't really do anything interesting with it: there's no juicy narrative to really explore why this is interesting, and it kinda feels like this just builds up to the mystery of who the director is in an unsatisfying way?

Or well, rather, it feels like this has two narrative threads: the exploration of the patients and the exploration of the hospital. The first feels like a very kinda, incohesive exploration of mental illness and the effects of the hospital; whereas the second really lets you just, explore a strange building and I guess my question is really: what's the focus here? What's the overall narrative arc of this piece?

I share EthanHanson's concerns about the Foundation using this to store anomalies: it feels like it's something plausible if they're a lot more confident about what this place is like; but it feels to me that the more interesting thing is exploring the foundation just having found it and like, really allowing the exploration of the place to let this shine.

Author, per the Draft Forum's policy: http://www.scp-wiki.net/forum/t-10629348/new-draft-forum-policies authors who have not yet posted a successful mainsite article are now required to get their basic concept(s) greenlighted by two experienced reviewers in the Ideas Critique forum and/or IRC chatrooms before asking for draft feedback.

Please first go to the Ideas forum or the chat, give a quick summary (for the Ideas forum, please follow the instructions in the required reading thread) of the concept you want to write up (don't link the draft unless someone requests it), and reviewers can help you make sure that your core idea is something that will be successful with the community audience.

During the conceptualization stage, reviewers can also help by letting you know if something similar already exists on the site, and/or telling you if there are any cliches/pitfalls/other typical downvote reasons to be careful of with your particular idea. These issues are more effectively addressed earlier on in the writing process.

If you have already received the requisite greenlights, please note from whom and where you received them. If you would like to receive draft critique without going through the greenlighting process, please use the IRC chatrooms to request reviews.

item.title: Re: Imaginary Friends (Greenlight Wanted)
item.content:encoded:
Follows Foundation Researcher Mason Cooper as he attempts to find the Parents of Subject XXXX-7 before its too late, logs goes into Dr. Masons thoughts as he desperately tries to find a way to help Subject XXXX-7, who he had grown attached to.

My, concern with this as a narrative is that it feels like a very personal, intimate story, and it makes me wonder whether a tale from the perspective of Cooper would work better? It'd be easier to justify showing e.g. the mental state of Cooper directly that way, and would likely feel…less forced than if you had to write it as a SCP, particularly since there'd be a tendency for you to have to keep writing it in clinical tone.

Beyond this, my real concern is that I'm not sure if you have a good idea of how this investigation plays out: what are the core plot beats? How are you intending to ramp up this tension? Does Mason succeed or fail?

item.title: Re: Seeking Greenlight: The Architects Automaton
item.content:encoded:
[+] Open for crit
– hide block

However, it has been discovered through intense physical manipulation and scientific reasoning, that SCP-XXXX will respond to particular audio frequencies, all of which are outside the audible spectrum. It will then activate autonomously and begin drawing with extreme precision until its internal potential energy is exhausted.

To be clear: it activates if the crank is turned and not just if you like, ask it via particular audio frequencies? If so, what does 'will respond to' mean?

Though the Architect's whereabouts and physicality are yet unknown, there are many strange, otherworldly objects that lend themselves to prove his existence.

Not really a fan of this angle. It feels too much like you're just throwing out a bunch of vague ideas you find kinda interesting in an attempt to make the position of the Architect more interesting; but it doesn't really and it doesn't really come across as interesting to me. More to the point, I'm not really sure how the Foundation figure out the Architect exists or like,,,what that actually means for this SCP or the world at large?

It has been noted that attempting to investigate and calculate these geometric patterns will result in Dissociative Amnesia, Psychosis, Dementia, Alzheimer's syndrome, and many other effects.

Generally I'm not a fan of things that just make you go crazy, particularly in a way that causes you to forget a lot; since like…it's super overplayed and often feels…kinda problematic and like it stigmatises mental illness more.

More to the point, it's also an effect that's really hard to convey in an interesting way within the confines of a SCP article.

It is not yet known what happens when SCP-XXXX is allowed to finish one of its patterns, but it is certainly best left to conjecture.

so like…what happens if it completes a pattern? How are you wanting to make this mystery interesting?

My central concern with this article is that feels like it lacks cohesion: there's a lot of elements here (the architect, the madness, the patterns it draw being ominous in some way, the otherworldly objects the architect made) but I don't really see how they all come together to tell a compelling story. I am also concerned that the Foundation are barely mentioned here: a SCP article is told from their perspective, and they don't seem to really have any kind of role in this story, or any real effect on how it plays out, and a very passive point of view like this can be really hard to do well.

item.title: Re: Seeking greenlights (Ghost Rider)
item.content:encoded:
[+] Open for crit
– hide block

This feels very much like it's a general haunted car idea and I don't really vibe with it as a result. Tying in this Doctor Danny as the driver and giving him dementia so he's unaware of the events feels…unsatisfying too because it adds more complexity to the idea but without really like…allowing you to explore any aspect of this. Like, if Danny was at least aware of what was happening, you could explore why he does this but he isn't and so you can't and so he might as well not be here?

Moving past this: it's always a red flag to me when someone writes a pitch for a SCP article and barely mentions the Foundation in their central narrative. A SCP article is told from the perspective of the Foundation, and is generally about what they do with the SCP and how they interact with it (and how it makes life hard for the Foundation), and so…the focus on like using the narrative section to passively reel off what the SCP does and how it affects people, and like, focus on the story of Danny becoming the driver feels like a mistake. Primarily this is because you can't actually include a lot of this in the SCP article, but it's also because even the parts you can end up feeling temporally remote from the actual events.

My advice would be to really consider why this is specifically a SCP article: what about this being a SCP and featuring the Foundation is interesting? What does doing it this way allow you to do beyond just writing it as a short story from the perspective of e.g. an omniscient narrator or Dr. Danny?

It might also be worth considering why this happens: what's the motivation of Danny here? What's the motivation of the car? Why do they go out every night? I don't think this necessarily has to be explicit in the article but I do think it would help you frame the conflict between the Foundation and the SCP.

item.title: Re: Blood Rose
item.content:encoded:
[+] Open for crit

A flower, specifically a rose, that possesses an olfactory cognitohazard that causes anyone that smells it to self-harm and "water" it with there own blood, killing themselves.

This feels…kinda edgy and also a little insensitive towards folk who self harm; but I think the bigger issue is that the compulsion effect means you're removing a lot of the opportunity to explore why someone would choose to water the flower with blood.

Beyond this, everything just feels…like it happens exactly as you'd expect? The foundation sends an MTF in and they're affected by the anomaly and do…exactly what the description says they'll do; and then there's a log indicating that like it turns out the flower has done exactly what the description says it'll do to a bunch of other people.

This feels like it needs…some kinda subversion or like, deeper exploration of how they managed to contain this or something: SCP-3597 is a good example of how this can be done; though there's a lot of ways you could explore it.

You mention in the hook that the flower contains 'the history of all it's victims': maybe there's an interesting historical angle you could take this on then? Like, perhaps if the flower was considered a holy object or something and people worshipped it and were affected by it to a lesser extent and then gradually it got more powerful or something.

item.title: Re: Lucky Rope
item.content:encoded:
1) You may want to kill part of the summary; mods tend to frown on entries that take up too much space on the screen. Also, it's "The Foundation", not "the foundation".

2) Your "Hook" Is just more description. It's supposed to describe why people care about the SCP, and what it's role in things is; that is, why the thing matters. Move what you have to the Central Narrative part and give us a reason to care about this guy (like the last sentence of the Narrative, emphasizing that sometimes it takes an SCP to deal with an SCP).

3) You need to decide between making this guy covert or having him show up on every sensor on the planet. Two stars and a black hole, if that's literal, make him a high threat to the very existence of those around him, if not the rest of the planet, and he would definitely not be allowed on field missions if that's the case.

More to the point, if this guy is supposed to handle the more powerful SCPs, then he is unlikely to do so without those around him dying or creating a distraction as he tries to save them. If he's at that power level, then he is a solo agent; he has to be because no one else would survive the very missions he would be needed on.

In all honesty, The Foundation has better use for this guy than rescue missions if he's a "galaxy figure".

Conversely, if his power is just luck (or one heck of a simulation of that), then he doesn't need all of the stars and black hole as those make him extremely dangerous.

Overall, it's not a bad idea, but you need to decide on what he is: He can't be a powerful entity with two stars and a black hole AND a covert SCP.

item.title: An uncommon network of tunnels
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights

Page Type: SCP Article

Genre: Suspense and adventure (not sure what it may be)

Page Layout:
Containment procedures and description; followed by in-depth information, such as exploration logs, interviews, related documents or tests, which present events in a non-linear sequence. The page may use darker (in color) elements for ambiance sake (in regards to in-universe design and narrative support).
In-depth information may be organized in different parts with a ListPages module or any other medium for focusing.

Elevator Pitch:

► A mostly subterranean network of tunnels that has the following properties
▼ A mostly subterranean network of tunnels that has the following properties:
  • Inner distances (mainly the longitudinal extension) and shapes of some tunnels don't match those expected by outside measurements, especially in underground ones.
  • Various tunnels lead to impossible locations, such as the end of other tunnel, structures not existing outside the network or different realities.
  • It connects (not necessarily directly) to odd places of different nature and varying degrees of relation with each other.
  • It appears to be infinite in size and has entrances all around the world.
  • Network and attached rooms are occupied by diverse kinds of entities, items and information. They are not always hostile or sentient but inherently imply a risk.
  • Anomalous events occur within the complex; for example, reality-based, space-time and biological distortions.
  • Antimemetic and physical qualities affect the network so that all attempts to bring logic to the spatial paradox meet failure.

Central Narrative:
After the containment procedures and the description are told, the article will focus on the experiences around this SCP and the hidden history of the places "inside" it.

► This second part of the article will relate this information in the form of records
▼ This second part of the article will relate this information in the form of records,

for instance, the incidents lived and findings made by separate Foundation teams on exploration procedures, the speech of sapient beings inhabiting the tunnels, the unraveling of the stories of the facilities connected to the network; going from initial approaches upon discovery, up to how a guide-rope tied to an agent (who ventured into the tunnels) conducts to the corpse of the latter, despite she exited through the other end of a tunnel alive and tied to the guide-rope.

Hook/Attention-Grabber:

► The "heart" of this concept is the in-depth data
▼ The "heart" of this concept is the in-depth data,

because of its significance for the article and how it is presented as a set of mysteries revolving around these places, which are features that, to my knowledge, are not prominent in the wiki.
All of this written as Foundation registries and excerpts from independent documents, having both clinical and literary tone. That is, the capacity of an informative text to not only tell data, but also narrate a story.

Additional Notes:
My major concerns are on the literary emphasis of the SCP, since I wouldn't like to create a tale made into an article. Keep in mind the concept is intended to form an actual SCP article, not a tale page designed as one.

item.title: The Bargainer
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights: Yes

Page Type: SCP Article

Elevator Pitch: a living humanoid mummy that can give you anything you want if you give it something it views as being equal in value.

Central Narrative: so far mostly just a series of tests on the SCPs abilities.

Hook/Attention-Grabber: The Bargainer is an advanced level reality warper with near omnipotent reality warping abilities, the only limits are that it can only use it's powers to keep up it's end of a bargain or protect itself. the SCP refuses to be given anything other than food for free, and will only accept personal belongings if it gives you give it something else in return. The Bargainer has a very primitive and basic understanding of monetary value, recognizing things like live humans, art, music, weapons, livestock, precious metals, and gems as been valuable, but doesn't understand the value of modern technologies, believing a sword that belonged to Genghis Khan is of equal value to a nuclear bomb. The SCP has a collection of personal belongings it has gained through trading with the foundation from tests, some of these items are; a sword from Genghis Khan, a palace (which acts as the containment cell) 20 beautiful maidens (20 conventionally attractive female personnel and D-Class who have never had sex), a David Bowie album, and a flock of chickens. The female personnel after living with the SCP for a month have mentioned that the SCP never attempted anything remotely sexual, and seems to just enjoy having company.

Additional Notes: I'm worried that the narrative I have right now isn't enough for this concept, but I'm not sure what else I could do narrative wise. The SCP avoids talking outside of bargains, due to how deteriorated it's throat is. I also felt like the limitations placed on it's abilities would help differentiate it from other reality warpers, what do you think?

item.title: SCP idea, Seeking Greenlights
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights: Yes

Page Type: SCP Article

Page Layout: I will use the regular format. Information will be presented in the form of interviews, procedures, detailed descriptions and firsthand accounts.

Elevator Pitch: It is a mechanical humanoid woman who has a large hatch in her stomach. Occasionally the hatch will open and a roughly head-sized block of wood drops out. The robot woman then sits down at a table to work and bites chunks into the wood block. Over time over time she will sculpt a figurine from the block, all the leftover material having been ingested by her. Most of the figurines she makes are very creepy and each is it's own sub-scp with their own anomalous properties themed around different mental illnesses. She continues doing this until the entire block has been used up at which point she consumes all her creations and starts the process again.

Central Narrative: As hinted at above, this scp is themed around mental illnesses and what would it be like if they were to take a physical form. They are intended to be the embodiment of those health conditions with the figurines linked to the most common mental illnesses appearing most often. It is not going to be blatantly obvious that any of this is the case like 'oh this one makes you feel depressed, this one gives you schizophrenia', each figurine is intended to appear as it's own interesting anomaly to a surface level reader while to someone with a keener eye the symbolism behind each doll will be apparent for them to see.

Hook/Attention-Grabber: First off I am not aware of any other robotic humanoids that eject a block of material from their body to sculpt small figurines out of so as far as I know it is very unique and different. Secondly I plan to create a wide variety of figurines that this scp has made which will allow for people to come up with theories and ideas for them and due to their large number there is likely to be at least one or two someone will find interesting.

Additional Notes: I could use some help coming up with a name. So far I've considered all the generic ones like Dollmaker, Sculptor, Sculptor's Handmaid, etc. but none of them are that good. If anyone has some more unorthodox ideas then don't be afraid to mention them.

item.title: SCP Concept: Guitar Hero
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights: Yes

Page Type: SCP Article

Genre (Optional): Horror

Page Layout (Optional): Standard layout

Elevator Pitch: SCP-XXXX consists of two components, SCP-XXXX-1 which is a seemingly normal electric guitar and SCP-XXXX-2 which is an also seemingly normal amplifier. However, SCP-XXXX-2 has a unique connector only compatible with SCP-XXXX-1 that is unable to be unplugged on SCP-XXXX-2’s end. There is also no external power in the form of an electrical cable or battery compartment, but the power level seems to be associated with a colored light next to the connector port.

Central Narrative: SCP-XXXX-1 first appears to its victim at random. It appears to be an ordinary guitar, but when played it gives its victim talent far beyond their own, allowing them to play any song, chord, or note by simply thinking of it. In addition, SCP-XXXX-1’s strings release an endorphin-like substance referred to as SCP-XXXX-ɑ that, when absorbed through the victim’s fingers, releases a feeling of euphoria and an increased desire to use SCP-XXXX-1. If the person tries it, after several days SCP-XXXX-2 will appear in the same manner as SCP-XXXX-1.

+ show block
– hide block

If SCP-XXXX-1 is ignored, rather than SCP-XXXX-2 appearing, SCP-XXXX-1 will disappear before revealing itself to a new victim. If SCP-XXXX-1 is plugged into SCP-XXXX-2, SCP-XXXX-2 seems to enter an active state. After a seemingly random number of uses, SCP-XXXX-2 will suddenly attack the victim, striking them in the throat with its connector. It lodges into the throat below the vocal cords. SCP-XXXX-2 will then broadcast the inner thoughts of the victim. It will attempt to draw out thoughts that are embarrassing or hurtful, and will then feed off the negative emotions of the host. The light on SCP-XXXX-2 will gradually change from its current state to a bright green as it absorbs emotions, and when it has fully fed off the victim and is fully charged, the adapter will be removed and the victim left to bleed out as both objects teleport away to repeat the cycle. It is currently unknown where or how SCP-XXXX-2 uses stored energy and needs to recharge between victims. In extreme cases, the light flashes a deep red and SCP-XXXX-2 has been known to attack seemingly without activation by SCP-XXXX-1 in a desperate attempt to sustain itself. It is currently unknown what will happen if SCP-XXXX-2 is completely drained of power, and until containment procedures are considered adequate any experimentation on that subject has been banned by the Foundation for fear of any of SCP-XXXX's unknown anomalous effects.

Hook/Attention-Grabber: The SCP chooses victims based on interaction, and simply ignoring it is enough to spare oneself from falling victim to it. The Safe-class component of the object is used to attract and serve as bait for the Euclid-class portion of the SCP. It is capable of teleportation, and so containment proves difficult as someone, usually D-class personnel, must routinely interact with SCP-XXXX-1 which will inherently draw SCP-XXXX-2 to it, but the two must never be allowed to be used together. When SCP-XXXX-2 appears in SCP-XXXX-1's containment chamber, any personnel in the room are to be immediately evacuated and anyone who had contact with SCP-XXXX-1 is to be put into quarantine while a containment team returns SCP-XXXX-2 to its original containment.
